title: Antigravity: Code With an AI Workforce
description: Learn Google's agent-first IDE: run multiple AI agents in parallel, review their work through artifacts, and ship software with an AI team under your command.

lessons.title: Google's Agent-First IDE
lessons.bodyMd:
## A new kind of code editor

In late 2025, Google released Antigravity, a code editor built around a simple bet: the future of programming is not a developer typing with an AI assistant looking over their shoulder. It is a developer managing a team of AI agents that do the typing.

That is what "agent-first" means. In a traditional editor, you write code and the AI helps. In Antigravity, you describe outcomes and AI agents plan, write, test, and revise the code, while you direct, review, and approve. You move from player to coach.

## Built on familiar ground

If you have used VS Code, Antigravity will feel like home. It is a VS Code fork, so the file explorer, terminal, extensions, and keyboard shortcuts all work the way you expect. Google did not reinvent the editor. They reinvented what happens inside it.

Under the hood it is Gemini-native: deeply integrated with Google's Gemini models, including very large context windows (around a million tokens, roughly thousands of pages of code at once). That huge context is what lets agents hold an entire project in mind instead of just the file you have open.

## The core unit: workspaces and agents

Antigravity organizes work differently from other AI editors. Instead of one chat panel helping with whatever file is open, you get:

* **Workspaces:** dedicated working areas, each with its own task and context.
* **Agents:** AI workers assigned to workspaces. You can run several at once.
* **The Agent Manager:** a mission-control view where you see every agent, what it is doing, and how far along it is.

Picture it like this: instead of one assistant sitting next to you, you have a small team in separate rooms, each working on an assignment, and you walk the hallway checking on them. That hallway is the Agent Manager.

## Agents that can use a browser

One standout capability: Antigravity agents can launch and control a real Chrome browser. They can load your app, click through it, take screenshots, and verify their own work visually. An agent that builds a landing page can open it, notice the spacing is off, and fix it without you saying a word. Agents can also use the browser for research and web scraping tasks.

## Who it is for

Antigravity targets developers who are ready to delegate: people building real projects who want leverage, not just autocomplete. It also appeals to ambitious beginners, because describing what you want in plain language is easier than writing every line yourself. But be honest with yourself about the tradeoff coming in the next lessons: you are trading direct control for leverage, and that demands a new skill, directing agents well.

## What this guide will teach you

Over four chapters you will install Antigravity and learn your way around, run your first agent task, master the plan-build-review workflow that makes agents reliable, parallelize work across multiple agents, and learn the honest limitations so you use the tool where it shines. Let's start by seeing how it compares to the alternatives.

lessons.title: Antigravity vs Cursor vs Windsurf
lessons.bodyMd:
## The three contenders

The agentic IDE space has three big names, each with a different philosophy. Understanding the differences helps you pick the right tool and use Antigravity for what it is actually best at.

## Cursor: the hybrid

Cursor is the most mature of the three, with a couple of years of agentic development behind it and the largest user base. Its philosophy is hybrid: powerful agent modes plus a full traditional IDE, so you never have to choose between working with agents and working yourself. You can run agents, watch diffs appear inline, jump in to edit CSS by hand, then hand control back.

* **Strengths:** maturity, reliability, huge community, model flexibility (Claude, GPT, and others), inline editing that keeps you in flow.
* **Tradeoffs:** one agent session at a time in the classic model, paid plans for serious use.

## Windsurf: the flow-state machine

Windsurf (from Codeium, now part of Cognition) is built around Cascade, its AI system that automatically pulls in relevant context from your whole project. The design goal is flow state: minimal UI friction, the AI quietly maintaining deep project understanding while you work.

* **Strengths:** automatic context handling, clean minimal interface, strong enterprise and compliance story, competitive pricing.
* **Tradeoffs:** single-session model like Cursor, less about orchestrating many agents.

## Antigravity: the agent orchestrator

Antigravity's defining difference is multi-agent orchestration. Where Cursor and Windsurf give you one powerful agent session, Antigravity gives you a team: multiple agents working in parallel across workspaces, overseen from the Agent Manager. Its transparency model is artifacts (plans, task lists, screenshots, recordings) rather than just inline diffs.

* **Strengths:** parallel agents, huge Gemini context window, integrated browser automation, artifact-based transparency.
* **Tradeoffs:** newest and least proven, Google ecosystem lean, reviewers note rough edges.

## Side-by-side

| | Antigravity | Cursor | Windsurf |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base | VS Code fork | VS Code fork | VS Code fork |
| Agent model | Multiple parallel agents | Single agent sessions + inline | Single Cascade session |
| Context | 1M tokens (Gemini) | Deep, model-dependent | Auto-retrieved (Cascade) |
| Browser control | Built in (Chrome) | Limited | Limited |
| Transparency | Artifacts: plans, screenshots, task lists | Real-time diffs, inline suggestions | Step-by-step workflow view |
| Best for | Parallel workstreams, delegation | Solo devs who want control + agents | Flow-state coding, enterprise teams |

## Which should you pick

Honest guidance, not fanboyism:

* **Solo developer on a complex project who likes staying hands-on:** Cursor's maturity is hard to beat.
* **Enterprise or regulated industry:** Windsurf's compliance story matters.
* **You want to delegate chunks of work to several agents at once:** Antigravity is the only one built for that.
* **You are learning and experimenting:** Antigravity launched free in public preview, which makes it a cheap way to learn agentic workflows.

Many developers end up using more than one. The skills transfer: learning to direct agents well in Antigravity makes you better at prompting Cursor's agents too. The next lesson helps you decide if Antigravity fits your situation.

lessons.title: When Antigravity Is the Right Choice
lessons.bodyMd:
## Great fits

**Greenfield projects.** Starting something new is where parallel agents shine. One agent scaffolds the backend, another builds the landing page, a third writes the initial tests. You define the shape; they fill it in simultaneously.

**Parallel workstreams.** Refactoring authentication while building a new API endpoint while updating docs: three independent tasks, three agents, one afternoon. If your work naturally splits into independent chunks, Antigravity multiplies you.

**Learning agentic workflows.** Because it launched free in public preview, Antigravity is a low-cost way to build the skill of directing AI agents: writing good task descriptions, reviewing plans, verifying outputs. That skill transfers to every AI tool you will touch for the rest of your career.

**Google-stack teams.** If your world is already Firebase, Google Cloud, and Gemini, Antigravity's native integrations remove friction. The browser automation pairs naturally with web apps deployed on Google infrastructure.

**Ambitious non-developers.** Founders and builders who can describe what they want clearly but do not write code daily can get further with a team of agents than with a blank editor. You still need to review and verify, but the leverage is real.

## Poor fits

**You need battle-tested stability.** Antigravity is the newest entrant. Reviewers consistently note rough edges: occasional instability, workflows that do not handle every situation gracefully. If you are shipping production code on a deadline tomorrow, a more mature tool is the safer pick.

**You dislike Google lock-in.** The deep Gemini and Google Cloud integration is a feature if you are in that ecosystem and a drawback if you are not. Teams standardized on other clouds or models may feel constrained.

**Quick single-file edits.** For "change this one function," the overhead of spinning up agents, workspaces, and artifacts is overkill. A lightweight editor with inline AI is faster.

**You want maximum direct control.** Some developers think best with hands on the keyboard. If delegating feels like losing the thread rather than gaining leverage, Cursor's hybrid model will suit you better.

## The honest summary

Antigravity is a bet on a specific future: developers as managers of agent teams. If that future excites you, there is no better tool to practice in, because no competitor commits to the multi-agent model as fully. If it makes you nervous, that is fine too. Start with small, low-stakes tasks, keep the plan-review habit from Chapter 3, and let trust build through verified results. The next chapter gets it installed and shows you around.

lessons.title: Installing Antigravity
lessons.bodyMd:
## Download

Head to antigravity.google and download the installer for your operating system (Windows, macOS, or Linux). It is a standard desktop install: download, run, follow the prompts. No command line needed.

## Sign in with Google

On first launch, Antigravity asks you to sign in with a Google account. This connects the IDE to Gemini models and your Google Cloud billing context. Use whatever Google account you want associated with your development work. If your team shares Google Workspace, check whether your organization has policies about AI coding tools before connecting a work account.

## System requirements

Antigravity is heavier than a plain text editor because it runs multiple AI agents, each holding large context. Practical minimums:

* **OS:** a recent version of Windows, macOS, or Linux (check the download page for specifics).
* **RAM:** 8 GB minimum, 16 GB recommended. Parallel agents each consume memory, and this is the most common bottleneck.
* **Disk:** a few GB for the app plus room for your projects.
* **Network:** a stable connection, since model calls go to Google's servers.

If your machine struggles, start with one agent at a time. The multi-agent fireworks can wait for better hardware.

## First launch

When Antigravity opens, you will see something reassuring: it looks like VS Code. File explorer on the left, editor in the middle, terminal at the bottom. Take a breath. You already know 80 percent of this interface.

What is new:

* **The agent panel:** where you describe tasks and chat with agents.
* **The Agent Manager:** the mission-control view for overseeing multiple agents (covered in the next lessons).
* **Artifacts:** plans, task lists, and screenshots agents produce as they work.

## Open a practice project

Do not point Antigravity at your most important codebase on day one. Create a small practice project instead: a simple personal website, a to-do app, a landing page for a fake business. You will make mistakes while learning (everyone does), and mistakes are free on a throwaway project.

```bash
mkdir ~/antigravity-practice
cd ~/antigravity-practice
```

Then open that folder in Antigravity (File, then Open Folder). You now have a blank canvas and a team of agents waiting for assignments. The next lesson tours the editor view; the one after introduces the Agent Manager where the real magic happens.
## A quick note on accounts and regions

Sign in with the Google account you want tied to your development work. If you have both a personal Gmail and a Google Workspace account through work, pick deliberately: billing, usage history, and any admin policies follow the account. Some Workspace organizations restrict AI coding tools, so a personal account is often the simpler choice for learning. Also note that availability and feature rollouts can vary by region while the product is in preview. If a feature described in this guide does not appear in your install, check for updates first before assuming it was removed.

lessons.title: The Editor View: Familiar Ground
lessons.bodyMd:
## Home sweet home

The editor view is Antigravity's VS Code inheritance: the file explorer, the code editor with syntax highlighting, the integrated terminal, the extensions marketplace, command palette, and all the keyboard shortcuts your muscle memory already knows. If you have customized VS Code with themes and extensions, much of that carries over or can be recreated in minutes.

This familiarity is strategic. Google wants the agent revolution to feel like an upgrade, not a relocation. You are not learning a new editor. You are learning new powers inside the editor you already know.

## Where the agents live in the editor

The main addition is the agent panel, typically docked on the side. This is where you:

* **Describe a task** in plain language ("add a contact form to the landing page that validates email addresses").
* **Chat with the working agent** to clarify, redirect, or answer its questions.
* **Watch progress** as it plans, writes files, and runs commands.
* **Review changes** before accepting them.

You will also see inline agent actions: the agent editing files shows up as changes you can review, much like a very fast pair programmer working in your editor while you watch.

## The terminal is still yours

The integrated terminal works exactly as before, and it matters more than ever. When an agent says "done," you verify in the terminal: run the tests, start the dev server, check the output. The agent proposes; the terminal disposes. Build the habit now: every agent task ends with you running something yourself to confirm it works.

## Extensions

The extensions marketplace works as in VS Code. Install your usual suspects: a formatter for your language (Prettier for JavaScript, Black or Ruff for Python), a linter, maybe a theme you like. Practical note: keep extensions lean at first. Every extension is another thing that can interact oddly with agent-driven edits. Add your full setup once you are comfortable with the agent workflow.

## The mindset shift

Here is the key mental adjustment for the editor view: **the editor is your cockpit, not your workshop.** In the old world, you built things here directly. In Antigravity, you increasingly direct from here while agents build in their workspaces. You still drop into the code to inspect, fix small things, and understand what was built. But your primary output shifts from keystrokes to decisions: what to build, whether the plan is right, whether the result is good.

That shift feels strange for about a week. Then it feels like leverage. The next lesson introduces the Agent Manager, which is where the directing happens.

lessons.title: The Agent Manager: Mission Control
lessons.bodyMd:
## The hallway with all the doors

The Agent Manager is Antigravity's signature view and the thing no competitor truly matches. It is a bird's-eye dashboard showing every agent you have running, which workspace each one is in, what task it is working on, and how far along it is. Think of it as the hallway with a window into every room where your team is working.

You can open it, scan the whole operation in seconds, and dive into any agent that needs attention. That overview is what makes managing parallel agents feasible. Without it, three agents would be chaos. With it, three agents are a team.

## Spawning agents

Creating an agent is deliberately lightweight:

1. Open the Agent Manager.
2. Create a new workspace (or pick an existing project folder).
3. Describe the task in plain language.
4. The agent starts working: reading the code, making a plan, executing.

Each agent operates in its own workspace with its own context, so agents do not step on each other's files. That isolation is what makes parallel work safe.

## A concrete example: three agents, one afternoon

Say you are building a small SaaS landing page with a signup backend. In the Agent Manager you spawn:

* **Agent A (frontend):** "Build a responsive landing page for a habit-tracking app: hero section, features grid, pricing table, footer. Use Tailwind. Match the style of the mockup in design-notes.md."
* **Agent B (backend):** "Create a signup API with email validation and a confirmation email. Node and Express. Store users in SQLite for now. Expose POST /api/signup."
* **Agent C (tests):** "Write integration tests for POST /api/signup covering valid signup, invalid email, and duplicate email."

Three rooms, three workers, one hallway. You check Agent B's plan, notice it missed rate limiting, and add it. You glance at Agent A's screenshots and approve the direction. Agent C finishes first and you review the tests while the others keep working.

## Watching without hovering

The Manager shows status at a glance: planning, executing, waiting for input, done. An agent that needs you (a question, an approval, an error it cannot resolve) flags itself. Your job is triage: most of the time, let them work. Intervene when flagged or when a periodic check shows drift.

Resist the urge to micromanage. Checking every thirty seconds breaks your own flow and does not make agents faster. Check on a rhythm: when one finishes, when one flags, or every 20 to 30 minutes.

## Workspaces explained

A workspace is more than a folder. It bundles the project files, the agent's task context, its artifacts (plans, screenshots, task lists), and its conversation history. When you revisit a workspace tomorrow, everything is where you left it: the plan, the progress, the open questions. Workspaces are also the unit of parallelism: one agent per workspace keeps concerns separated and prevents two agents from editing the same file in conflicting ways.

## Limits to respect

* **Your machine:** each agent consumes RAM and model context. Three to five parallel agents is the practical range on a good machine. More than that and everything slows down.
* **Your attention:** every agent you spawn is something you must eventually review. Do not spawn more agents than you can thoughtfully review. Unreviewed agent output is a liability, not an asset.
* **Task independence:** agents work best on independent tasks. If Agent B's API must match Agent A's frontend exactly, define the interface (the API contract) yourself first, then let them build to it in parallel.

The Agent Manager turns "AI helps me code" into "I run a team." The next lesson runs your first real task end to end.

lessons.title: Your First Agent Task
lessons.bodyMd:
## Pick something small and visible

For your first task, choose something with a visible result you can judge in thirty seconds. A landing page section, a small component, a script that does one thing. Avoid your production codebase, avoid anything with real user data, avoid tasks with five ambiguous requirements. You are learning the controls, not shipping.

Good first task for your practice project: "Add a hero section to the landing page with a headline, a subheadline, an email signup input, and a button. Make it responsive."

## Describe the task well

Open the agent panel, select your practice workspace, and write the task like a work order:

> Add a hero section to index.html for a habit-tracking app called Streakly.
> Include: a headline ("Build habits that stick."), a one-line subheadline,
> an email input with a "Get early access" button, and a simple responsive
> layout that stacks on mobile. Use Tailwind CSS via CDN. Keep the style
> minimal: dark background, white text, one accent color.

Notice what this includes: the file, the product name, every element, the layout behavior, the tech choice, and the style direction. Specificity is kindness to agents.

## Watch it work

The agent will typically go through visible phases:

1. **Explore:** reads the project files to understand what exists.
2. **Plan:** produces a short plan (this becomes an artifact you can review).
3. **Execute:** writes the code, possibly in several files.
4. **Verify:** may run checks or, with browser automation, load the page and screenshot it.

Do not interrupt the explore and plan phases. The most common beginner mistake is panic-typing "wait, also make the button blue" thirty seconds in. Let the plan land first, then redirect.

## Review the plan before the code

If the agent shows you a plan, read it. This is your cheapest intervention point. A plan that says "I will add the hero section to index.html using Tailwind classes" is fine. A plan that says "I will restructure the project into components" for a simple hero section is overengineering: redirect it now, in one sentence, before it writes a line.

## Review the result

When the agent finishes:

1. **Read the diff.** Look at what actually changed, file by file.
2. **Run it.** Start the dev server or open the page. Click the button. Resize the window.
3. **Check the requirements.** Every element you asked for, present and working? Mobile stacking correct?
4. **Fix or redirect.** Small issues you can fix yourself in the editor. Bigger misses get a follow-up message to the agent: "The button does nothing on click. Wire it to show a confirmation message."

## What you just learned

The full loop: describe precisely, let it plan, review the plan, let it build, verify yourself. Every advanced workflow in Chapter 3 is a variation on this loop: the planning lesson makes step 3 more rigorous, the parallel lesson runs several loops at once, the artifacts lesson makes review systematic, and the browser lesson automates part of verification. You now know the dance. Next chapter teaches the fancy footwork.

lessons.title: Planning First: Review Before You Build
lessons.bodyMd:
## The most valuable habit in agentic coding

Here is the workflow that separates people who love AI agents from people who complain about them: never let an agent write code before you have reviewed its plan. Five minutes of plan review saves thirty minutes of watching an agent confidently build the wrong thing.

## How to get a plan

Be explicit. Instead of "build user authentication," say:

> Before writing any code, create an implementation plan for adding email and password authentication to this project. Include: the files you will create or modify, the database schema changes, the routes, and how you will test it. Do not write code until I approve the plan.

The agent produces a plan artifact: a structured document listing steps, files, and decisions. This is now a thing you can read, critique, and approve, separate from the code itself.

## How to review a plan

Read it like a tech lead reviewing a junior developer's proposal. Check:

* **Scope:** does it do what you asked, no more and no less? Agents love to overbuild ("while I'm at it, I'll also add OAuth, roles, and..."). Trim ruthlessly.
* **File choices:** is it modifying the right files? Creating files in sensible places? If your project has conventions (routes in one folder, components in another), the plan should follow them.
* **Schema and API decisions:** these are the hardest to undo later. If the plan's data model looks wrong, fix it now.
* **Test plan:** "I will verify by..." should be concrete: run the test suite, load the page, hit the endpoint. Vague verification promises produce vague results.
* **Assumptions:** good plans state assumptions ("assuming SQLite is acceptable for now"). Challenge the ones you disagree with.

## The redirect

When the plan is off, redirect in plain language, one issue at a time:

> The plan looks good except: use our existing users table instead of creating a new one, and skip the password reset flow for now. Update the plan.

Let it revise the plan, re-review, and only then say "approved, build it." Two review rounds is normal. Five means the task was too big; split it.

## Why this works

Planning forces the agent to think before acting, which measurably improves output quality. It also forces you to think: reading a plan often surfaces requirements you had not articulated ("oh wait, I do need social login eventually, but not now"). The plan becomes shared understanding, and shared understanding is what makes delegation work, with humans or with AI.

## Make it the default

Put plan-first behavior in your project rules (Chapter 4, lesson 2): "For any task touching more than two files, produce an implementation plan and wait for approval before writing code." Once it is a rule, you stop having to remember to ask. The agent plans by default, and you review by default. That is the workflow.

lessons.title: Parallel Agents: Divide and Conquer
lessons.bodyMd:
## The superpower, used well

Parallel agents are Antigravity's headline feature, and they are genuinely transformative when the work splits cleanly. They are also the easiest feature to misuse. This lesson is about the difference.

## What parallelizes well

* **Independent features:** a settings page and a notifications system that do not share code.
* **Layers with a defined contract:** frontend and backend built against an API spec you wrote first.
* **Build plus verify:** one agent implements, another writes tests for the implementation.
* **Research plus build:** one agent investigates library options while another scaffolds the project.
* **Bulk independent chores:** updating dependencies across services, writing docs for five modules, translating UI strings.

The pattern: tasks that do not need to talk to each other while running.

## What does not parallelize well

* **Deeply coupled work:** two agents refactoring the same module will conflict, confuse each other, and produce a merge nightmare.
* **Sequential decisions:** if step B depends on a judgment call in step A, do not run them simultaneously. Run A, decide, then spawn B.
* **Exploratory work:** "figure out why the app is slow" needs one coherent investigation, not three competing theories.

When in doubt, ask: could I give these to three human developers without them needing a meeting? If yes, parallelize. If they would need to coordinate constantly, do not.

## The contract-first technique

The highest-leverage parallel pattern: you define the interface, agents build the sides. Example for a signup flow:

1. **You write the contract** (five minutes): `POST /api/signup` takes `{email, password}`, returns `{userId}` on success or `{error}` on failure. Frontend calls it from the signup form.
2. **Agent A** builds the backend endpoint to that contract.
3. **Agent B** builds the frontend form to that contract.
4. **Agent C** writes integration tests against that contract.

Nobody waits for anybody. The contract is the coordination. This is exactly how good engineering teams parallelize, and it works the same with agents.

## Running the operation

* **Spawn deliberately:** in the Agent Manager, create one workspace per task and assign. Name workspaces clearly ("signup-backend", "signup-frontend", "signup-tests").
* **Stagger the starts:** launch the most uncertain task first so its questions surface early while others are still warming up.
* **Triage, do not hover:** check the Manager on a rhythm. Let agents work; intervene on flags and drift.
* **Integrate at the end:** when agents finish, you do the final assembly: merge the branches or copy the pieces together, run the full test suite, and verify the whole thing works as one system. Integration is a human job. Do not delegate it.

## Know your limits

Practical ceiling: three to five agents on a good machine, fewer on modest hardware. But the real limit is review bandwidth. Every agent's output needs your eyes before it counts as done. Spawning six agents when you can only thoughtfully review three means three agents' work ships unverified, which is how bugs are born. Scale parallelism to your review capacity, not your CPU.

lessons.title: Artifacts: Trusting What the Agent Did
lessons.bodyMd:
## Show your work

When a human developer finishes a task, you can ask "walk me through what you did." Antigravity agents answer that question with artifacts: concrete byproducts of their work that let you verify instead of trust. Plans, task lists, implementation notes, screenshots, and browser recordings are all artifacts. Together they form a verifiable trail from your request to the finished code.

This is Antigravity's answer to the core anxiety of agentic coding: "the AI did something, but what exactly, and is it right?" Artifacts make the work inspectable.

## The artifact types you will see

* **Implementation plans:** the proposed approach, written before code. Your main review surface.
* **Task lists:** the agent's breakdown of the job into steps, with status. Useful for long tasks: you can see it is on step 6 of 9 and what remains.
* **Screenshots:** visual captures from the agent's browser automation. "Here is what the page looks like now."
* **Browser recordings:** sequences of browser actions the agent took while testing. Proof it actually clicked through the flow, not just claimed to.
* **Summaries:** end-of-task recaps: what changed, what was tested, what remains uncertain.

## The review workflow

Make artifact review a ritual, not a chore:

1. **Read the plan first** (before code exists). Approve or redirect.
2. **Skim the task list** during execution if the task is long. Confirm progress looks sane.
3. **Read the diff.** Artifacts supplement but never replace reading the actual code changes.
4. **Check the evidence.** Screenshots of the working UI, test output, browser recordings of the flow. Claims without evidence get verified by you, not believed.
5. **Run it yourself.** The terminal is the final artifact. Start the app, exercise the feature, confirm with your own eyes.

Steps 4 and 5 are where most people get lazy, and where most agent-introduced bugs slip through. The agent's screenshots show what it looked at; your own run shows what is actually true.

## Artifacts in your workspace

Many setups keep an `artifacts/` folder in the project for agent outputs: plans, logs, visuals. This is genuinely useful: next week, when you wonder "why did we build it this way," the plan artifact answers. Treat agent artifacts like design docs. They are the documentation of decisions, and future you will be grateful.

## Calibrating trust

The goal is calibrated trust, not blind trust or permanent suspicion. Early on, review everything closely. As an agent proves reliable on a class of tasks (say, writing straightforward CRUD endpoints), you can review those more lightly while staying rigorous on unfamiliar or high-stakes work (auth, payments, migrations). Trust is earned per task type, and artifacts are the evidence it is earned with. A year from now, you will still spot-check, because even good agents have bad minutes.

lessons.title: Browser Automation: Agents That Test Themselves
lessons.bodyMd:
## A browser the agent can drive

Antigravity agents can launch and control a real Chrome browser: navigate to URLs, click buttons, fill forms, take screenshots, and read what is on the page. This is not a simulation. It is an actual browser doing actual things, directed by the agent.

Why this matters: most software is ultimately judged through a browser. An agent that can open your app and look at it closes the loop between "I wrote code" and "it works." That loop used to require you. Now the agent can run it.

## The self-testing loop

Here is the workflow that browser automation enables:

1. The agent builds a landing page.
2. It launches Chrome, loads the page, and screenshots it.
3. It looks at the screenshot, notices the headline overlaps the image on mobile widths.
4. It fixes the CSS, reloads, screenshots again.
5. It reports done, with before and after screenshots as artifacts.

Steps 2 through 4 used to be your job. The agent doing its own visual QA is one of the most practical wins in Antigravity, especially for frontend work where "looks right" is the spec.

## What to ask for

Be explicit that you want browser verification:

> Build the pricing page, then open it in the browser, screenshot it at desktop and mobile widths, and fix any layout issues you see before reporting done.

Or for existing work:

> Open the signup flow in the browser and click through it as a new user. Report anything broken or confusing, with screenshots.

You can also point browser automation outward: "go to these three competitor pricing pages and summarize their tiers in a table." Research and scraping are legitimate uses, within the sites' terms of service.

## The supervision rule

A browser that can click can also submit, purchase, post, and delete. Treat browser automation like a very fast intern with your credit card: useful, but supervised. Rules:

* **Never let agents act on production systems unsupervised.** Testing happens on local or staging environments.
* **No real transactions.** Test checkouts with test mode, test accounts, and fake data.
* **Review before any outward action.** If the task involves posting, emailing, or publishing, the agent drafts and you approve.
* **Watch the first runs.** Until you trust an agent's browser judgment, keep its window visible and glance over.

## Where it struggles

Browser automation is impressive and imperfect. Agents can misread complex pages, get stuck on CAPTCHAs and login walls (correctly: those are there to stop automation), and burn a lot of time on fiddly interactions a human does in seconds. If an agent is flailing on a browser task for more than a few minutes, take over that step yourself and let the agent continue with the rest. The goal is leverage, not purity.

lessons.title: Writing Prompts Agents Actually Follow
lessons.bodyMd:
## Prompts are work orders

Every agent task starts with your description, and the quality of that description is the single biggest predictor of the result. Think of prompts as work orders you would hand a capable contractor: clear on the outcome, specific on the constraints, explicit about how you will judge the result.

## Bad vs good

**Bad:** "Make the signup page better."

Why it fails: better how? Visually? Faster? Higher converting? The agent guesses, and its guess will not match yours.

**Good:** "Redesign the signup page (signup.html): center the form vertically, increase input padding to 16px, add inline validation messages under each field that appear on blur, and make the submit button full-width on mobile. Keep the existing color scheme. Do not change the form fields or the submission endpoint."

Why it works: the file, every change, the constraints, and what not to touch. The agent has no decisions left except implementation details, which is exactly where you want its judgment.

**Bad:** "Add tests."

**Good:** "Add integration tests for POST /api/signup in tests/signup.test.js: valid signup returns 201 with a userId, invalid email returns 400, duplicate email returns 409. Use the existing test helpers in tests/helpers.js. Run the suite and confirm all pass."

## The anatomy of a strong task prompt

1. **Target:** the files, the feature, the area. ("In components/Header.jsx...")
2. **Outcome:** what done looks like, concretely. ("...add a mobile menu that slides in from the right.")
3. **Constraints:** tech choices, style rules, things not to change. ("Use Tailwind. Do not modify the desktop layout.")
4. **Acceptance criteria:** how you will verify. ("Verify by running npm test and loading the page at mobile width.")
5. **Context pointers:** where the relevant code or docs live. ("The API client is in lib/api.js; follow its patterns.")

You will not always need all five. Small tasks need two or three. But when a task goes wrong, the cause is almost always a missing element from this list.

## One task per agent

"Build the dashboard, fix the login bug, and update the docs" is three tasks wearing a trench coat. The agent will do the first well, the second hastily, and forget the third. Split compound requests into separate tasks, ideally separate agents. You get better results and cleaner artifacts, and each piece is independently reviewable.

## Point at things, do not describe vibes

"The header feels off" is a vibe. "The header logo is 8px too low relative to the nav links, and the spacing between links is inconsistent" is a pointer. When you can, reference exact files, line numbers, error messages, and screenshots. Paste the error text rather than summarizing it. Agents work with specifics far better than impressions.

## Iterate conversationally

The first result is a draft, not a verdict. Follow up like you would with a colleague: "closer, but the button should be blue to match the brand, and the form needs a loading state on submit." Short, specific corrections beat long re-explanations. And when the agent nails it, say so. Positive feedback on what "right" looks like helps it calibrate to your taste over time.

lessons.title: Rules and Project Context
lessons.bodyMd:
## Stop repeating yourself

If you find yourself typing "remember, we use TypeScript strict mode" or "don't touch the legacy folder" in every task prompt, that information belongs in project rules: standing instructions the agent reads automatically at the start of every task. Write once, benefit forever.

## Where rules live

Antigravity reads project-level agent instructions from configuration files in your project. The community convention includes:

* **`.antigravity/rules.md`:** Antigravity's native rules file. Standing instructions for agents working in this project.
* **`.cursorrules`:** the Cursor-compatible equivalent. Antigravity-aware workspace templates often include both so the project works across editors.

These are plain Markdown files. When an agent starts a task in your project, it ingests them as part of its context. Keep them short: agents follow five sharp rules better than fifty vague ones.

## What to put in rules

* **Stack and versions:** "Node 22, TypeScript strict, Tailwind v4, Prisma with Postgres."
* **Conventions:** "Components in components/, one per file, named exports. API routes in app/api/."
* **Commands:** "Run tests with npm test. Typecheck with npm run typecheck. Never skip these before reporting done."
* **No-go zones:** "Do not modify anything under legacy/. Do not change the database schema without asking."
* **Workflow defaults:** "For tasks touching more than two files, produce an implementation plan and wait for approval first."
* **Style:** "Prefer small functions. No comments that restate the code. Error messages must be user-friendly."

## Example rules file

```markdown
# .antigravity/rules.md

## Stack
Node 22, TypeScript (strict), Tailwind v4, Next.js App Router, Prisma + Postgres.

## Conventions
- Components live in components/, one component per file, named exports.
- API routes live in app/api/ and always validate input with zod.
- Database access only through lib/db.ts, never raw SQL in routes.

## Commands
- Verify with `npm test` and `npm run typecheck` before reporting done.
- Never run `npm run build` while `npm run dev` is running (shared .next folder).

## Boundaries
- Do not touch anything under legacy/.
- Do not change the Prisma schema without explicit approval.
- Never commit or push. Leave changes uncommitted for review.

## Workflow
- Tasks touching more than two files: write an implementation plan first
  and wait for approval before coding.
- End every task with a summary: files changed, tests run, anything uncertain.
```

Notice the last rule: it makes the agent report like a professional. That summary is what you read first during review.

## Rules hygiene

* **Review quarterly.** Rules rot as projects evolve. A rule referencing a folder you deleted is worse than no rule: it confuses the agent.
* **Project rules over global habits.** Keep project-specific stuff in the project. Global preferences (your editor theme, your tone) do not belong here.
* **When an agent keeps making the same mistake,** do not just correct it in chat. Add a rule. Chat corrections evaporate; rules persist.

Good rules are the difference between an agent that needs constant supervision and one that works the way your team works. Thirty minutes writing rules pays back every single day.

lessons.title: Cost, Stability, and Honest Limitations
lessons.bodyMd:
## The fine print, up front

Antigravity is powerful, new, and imperfect. This lesson is the honest accounting: what it costs, where it is rough, and the habits that keep you safe while the product matures.

## Cost

Antigravity launched free during its public preview, which is a generous way to learn. Pricing for AI IDEs in this category has been moving (competitors sit roughly in the $10 to $25 per month range for paid tiers), and Google's plans may evolve. Check antigravity.google for current pricing before you build a workflow that depends on a specific tier. If you are on a free tier, learn whether it has usage caps so a big parallel session does not stall halfway.

## Stability: it is young

Antigravity is the newest major entrant in this space, and reviewers are consistent about the tradeoff: exciting capabilities, visible rough edges. Things users report include occasional instability during long sessions, agent confusion in complex situations, and gaps in workflows that mature tools handle smoothly (one reviewer noted limited git branch support as an example). None of this makes it unusable. It makes it a tool to use with the safety habits below, not blind trust.

Practical responses to youth:

* **Save and commit often.** Granular git commits are your time machine. If an agent session goes sideways, you revert to the last good commit instead of untangling the mess.
* **Keep tasks modest.** Smaller tasks fail smaller. A 20-file refactor that goes wrong is a disaster; four 5-file tasks are recoverable.
* **Update thoughtfully.** New versions bring fixes and new rough edges. Update, but re-verify your core workflow after updating.

## The safety habits

These apply to every agentic tool, doubly to a young one:

1. **Never let agents push to shared branches unsupervised.** Agents work locally; humans merge. "Never commit or push" belongs in your rules file.
2. **No real data in agent experiments.** Test with fixtures and seed data, never production databases or real user accounts.
3. **Review every diff.** Artifacts help, but the diff is ground truth. No diff review, no merge.
4. **Run the tests yourself.** The agent's "all tests pass" claim gets verified in your terminal.
5. **Keep secrets out of prompts.** API keys go in env files and secret managers, never in task descriptions. Prompts get logged; env files do not.

## Calibrating expectations

Antigravity today is best thought of as a force multiplier for developers who already know how to judge code, not a replacement for that judgment. It makes a good developer dramatically faster and a careless one dramatically more productive at producing bugs. The developers who get the most from it share three traits: they write precise task descriptions, they review plans before code, and they verify everything themselves. Those are exactly the habits this guide teaches.

## The workflow that works

If you take one thing from this guide, take this loop: describe precisely, require a plan, review the plan, parallelize independent work, review artifacts and diffs, verify in your terminal, commit granularly. Do that consistently and Antigravity becomes what it promises to be: not an autopilot, but a team. And you are a good manager.
